subject: chemistry
question_text: Define IE₁ and IE₂. Why is IE₂ > IE₁ for a given atom? Discuss the factors that affect the ionisation enthalpy of an element.

verification.note: Chapter 2 is sourced from the Sri Chaitanya Junior Fastrack chemistry section (book pp.53-55), which prints the question, its star rank and a model answer. Only ONE source book is held for chemistry — the TSBIE Basic Learning Material in hand covers physics only — so the two-book union check is PENDING a second chemistry source. The 1+1+2+4 mark split is a CLAIM until a Telangana IPE teacher confirms it; the question itself is sourced, not invented. WORDING: the book's 'factors that effect IE' is regularised to affect. The book writes the factor relations as proportionalities (I.E ∝ 1/atomic size, I.E ∝ nuclear charge, I.E ∝ 1/screening effect); these are qualitative shorthands for trends, not numerical laws, and the card keeps them with that reading. The book's reason for IE₂ > IE₁ — 'in unipositive ion number of protons are more than the number of electrons, so the nuclear attraction increases' — is essentially right and the card states it precisely: the same nuclear charge acts on one electron fewer. AI chemistry check 2026-08-25: both definitions, the IE₂ > IE₁ reason and all four factors re-checked against NCERT Class-11; no chemistry changed; one memory tip reworded to plain literal language. Status stays unverified.

page_header: Classification of Elements – Periodic Properties · 8 marks

steps.label: Defining IE₁
lines: IE₁ (first ionisation enthalpy): the energy
required to remove an electron from the
outermost orbital of an isolated neutral
gaseous atom.
steps.why: Each qualifier closes a loophole: isolated rules out neighbours, gaseous rules out lattice energies, neutral marks this as the first removal. The equation states the same definition in symbols.
common_mistakes: Dropping isolated, gaseous or neutral from the definition. All three are marked words.
Writing the equation without (g). The state symbol is part of the definition.
steps.memory_tip: One lone gas atom, one electron taken from its outer shell — that energy is IE₁.
steps.margin_note: Definition in words plus the equation; the same pattern repeats for IE₂.

steps.label: Defining IE₂
lines: IE₂ (second ionisation enthalpy): the energy
required to remove an electron from the
unipositive gaseous ion.
steps.why: The second ionisation starts from X⁺, not from the atom — writing the starting species correctly is what the definition is testing.
common_mistakes: Starting the IE₂ equation from X(g). It starts from X⁺(g).
Writing X²⁻ or a wrong charge on the product. Removing an electron from X⁺ gives X²⁺.
steps.memory_tip: IE₂ starts where IE₁ ended: the ion X⁺ loses the next electron.
steps.margin_note: Check the charges balance across the arrow: +1 on the left, +2 and −1 on the right.

steps.label: Why IE₂ > IE₁
lines: In the ion X⁺ the number of electrons is one
less than the number of protons.
The same nuclear charge now acts on fewer
electrons, so each remaining electron is held
more strongly, and the ion is smaller than
the atom.
Removing the second electron therefore needs
more energy: IE₂ > IE₁.
steps.why: Nothing about the nucleus changes between the two removals — what changes is the electron count. Fewer electrons under the same pull means each one is held more strongly, and a strongly held electron needs more energy to remove.
common_mistakes: Writing that the nuclear charge increases after ionisation. The proton count never changes; the electron count falls.
Giving the fact IE₂ > IE₁ without the fewer-electrons reason. The reason carries both marks.
steps.memory_tip: Same pull, fewer electrons to share it — every remaining electron is held more strongly, so the second removal needs more energy.
steps.margin_note: Two marks sit on this paragraph; the smaller-ion sentence strengthens it.

steps.label: Factor 1 — atomic size
lines: Factors affecting ionisation enthalpy:
1. Atomic size: as the atomic size increases,
the outer electron lies farther from the
nucleus, and I.E decreases.
steps.why: The attraction between nucleus and electron falls with distance, so a larger atom releases its outer electron for less energy. The ∝ line is shorthand for this inverse trend.
common_mistakes: Writing the proportionality the wrong way up. Bigger atom, lower I.E.
Stating the trend without the distance reason.
steps.memory_tip: Distance weakens the pull: the farther the electron, the less energy its removal needs.
steps.margin_note: Four numbered factors, one mark each; keep each to two lines and its relation.

steps.label: Factor 2 — nuclear charge
lines: 2. Nuclear charge: as the nuclear charge
increases (at nearly the same size), the outer
electrons are pulled in more strongly, and
I.E increases.
steps.why: More protons means a stronger pull on every electron, so more energy is needed to remove one — the direct partner of the size factor.
common_mistakes: Confusing nuclear charge with ionic charge. Nuclear charge is the proton count Z.
Writing an inverse relation here. Nuclear charge and I.E rise together.
steps.memory_tip: Size and charge pull the ionisation enthalpy in opposite directions: size lowers it, charge raises it.
steps.margin_note: This is the only direct (not inverse) relation among the four factors.

steps.label: Factor 3 — screening effect
lines: 3. Screening effect: the inner-shell electrons
reduce the nuclear pull on the outer electron.
The greater the screening, the lower the I.E.
steps.why: Screening cancels part of the nuclear charge before it reaches the outer electron, so it works against the pull and lowers the cost of removal.
common_mistakes: Writing that screening increases I.E. More screening means a weaker hold and a lower I.E.
Attributing the screening to outer electrons. The inner shells do the screening.
steps.memory_tip: Screening is the nuclear charge factor in reverse: whatever the inner shells cancel, the outer electron never feels.
steps.margin_note: This factor links back to the very short answer question on the screening effect.

steps.label: Factor 4 — electronic configuration
lines: 4. Electronic configuration: half-filled and
completely filled orbitals are extra stable, so
atoms having them need more energy to lose
an electron.

lines.text: Half-filled or completely filled orbitals → extra stability → higher I.E

lines: Example: N (2p³, half-filled) has a higher
IE₁ than O (2p⁴).
steps.why: A stable arrangement takes extra energy to break, so stability shows up directly as a higher ionisation enthalpy — the factor that explains the exceptions the first three factors cannot.
common_mistakes: Leaving out this fourth factor and listing only three.
Giving the N and O comparison the wrong way. Nitrogen's half-filled 2p³ makes its IE₁ the higher one.
steps.memory_tip: A half-filled 2p³ and a completely filled 2p⁶ are extra stable, so removing an electron from either needs more energy.
steps.margin_note: The N versus O example is the standard illustration and is worth the one extra line.

insider_note: Three separate asks share these eight marks — definitions, the IE₂ > IE₁ reason, and the four factors — and the reason paragraph is where students most often write the fact without the fewer-electrons argument that carries its two marks.
